Bangalore, late 1990s. Four professors who decided PCs were the wrong answer.

Inside the Indian Institute of Science, in the Department of Computer Science and Automation, 4 faculty members - Vijay Chandru, Swami Manohar, Ramesh Hariharan, and V Vinay were running a small industry-facing lab called Percolat, doing contract research projects. 

Nothing unusual about that. Profs do consulting work all the time....

But somewhere in the middle of it, 1 particular side-project quietly took over their imaginations: an idea for a device built specifically for the common man of the developing world.

In a country of a billion+ people, computers were expensive, English-centric, keyboard-dependent, and utterly useless to anyone who could not read. 

At the time, only 9/1000 Indians owned a computer....

So they asked a different question entirely: what if a computer did not need you to read / type / even own it yourself?

They called it the Simputer and get this, they liked the name so much they built the meaning backward to fit it: 

the Simputer Trust framed it as short for "Simple, Inexpensive, and Multilingual" computer.

The vision, boldly printed on their launch T-shirts, was just 2 words: "Radical simplicity." 🙏🙏

The scientists literally wore that phrase "for universal access" on jeans and tees at the launch event.

No keyboard. No literacy required. No ownership required.

This is where the Simputer stops being just "a cheap Indian gadget" and becomes genuinely visionary. 

Look at what they actually engineered:

- No keyboard: just a touchscreen and a stylus, because a farmer should not need to learn QWERTY to use a computer.

- Text to speech in local languages: the device could speak the screen's contents aloud, so an illiterate user in the literal, not metaphorical sense could still operate it. 

- A device you did not need to own: this is the masterstroke. The Simputer used cheap removable memory cards nicknamed "Chikki" cards, so a whole village could share one physical Simputer, while each person carried their own low cost card holding their personal data. One machine, many owners, zero exclusion. 

- Fully open hardware: years before "open source hardware" was even a phrase people used casually, the Simputer's entire hardware specification was released under its own license, the Simputer General Public License, explicitly inspired by the free software movement. Anyone, anywhere, could legally build one. 

Think about the audacity of that last point. A team of Indian academics open-sourced the blueprint of a computer, in 2001, so the idea could outlive any one company.

April 25, 2001. Bangalore shows the world....

The 1st working Simputer prototypes were unveiled on the 25th of April, 2001, built on a shoestring, quite literally by hand. The team had bought exactly one StrongARM processor board from the US to prototype with, Vinay wrote the software, and Manohar personally burned it onto the chip's memory. 

No massive R&D budget. No corporate lab. Just profs doing hardware bring-up like hobbyists, because that is what building the future from scratch actually looks like. 

The world noticed almost immediately. By December 2001, the New York Times named the Simputer the biggest technological innovation of the year. 

In 2002, it won the 1st ever Dewang Mehta Award for innovation in IT from India's own Ministry of Information Technology. 

The profs did not stop at invention. With the institute's blessing, they did something almost nobody had done from inside an Indian academic institution before: they spun their research into companies. 

Strand Life Sciences launched in Nov 2000, and Picopeta Simputers followed in May 2001 becoming, together, the 1st examples of academic entrepreneurship to come out of IISc. 

That single decision, profs stepping off the tenure track to build a company around their own invention quietly rewired what was considered possible at Indian institutions. 

It is credited with pioneering faculty entrepreneurship at IISc, a precedent that IITs and other institutions would go on to follow. 

By 2004, the commercial version, the Amida Simputer, finally hit the market: a $220 handheld with a 206 MHz processor, 64MB of memory, a monochrome touchscreen, a 6 hour battery, and full internet connectivity, running Linux to keep licensing costs at zero. 

Bharat Electronics Limited even stepped in as a manufacturing partner, branding it the BEL-PicoPeta Simputer. 

It should have been everywhere. It was mot. 

Software developers struggled to build applications for a device this different, distributors did not know how to sell something so unfamiliar, and the govt never placed the bulk order that could have jump started an app ecosystem. 

A change in leadership at BEL eventually brought production to a quiet halt altogether. 

When Bill Gates visited Bangalore in 2005, he was directly asked about the Simputer's potential and by Vinay's account, senior design engineers working on the iPhone had studied the Simputer for ideas years before Apple's device ever shipped. 

A handheld, touchscreen first, stylus-operated, always-connected personal computing device, engineered in Bangalore for illiterate rural users years before Silicon Valley made "mobile-first" a religion. 

The Simputer did not win the market. But it got the idea right long before the world was ready to listen.

That is the story people mean when they whisper, half-joking, half-serious: before the iPhone, there was the Simputer.

Prompt for AI video generation (Runway / Kling / Luma / Hailuo / etc.)

A vertical 9:16 cinematic AI art video, 10 seconds long, smooth continuous morphing transformation of a hyper-detailed surreal fashion portrait of a beautiful woman.

The face is always split vertically down the middle: left side porcelain-white skin with icy blue eyes and glossy red lips, right side deep matte black skin with glowing red eyes and metallic silver lips. High-fashion editorial beauty, sharp features, intense gaze looking straight at camera.

Throughout the video the face constantly shatters and recomposes with floating geometric fragments: sharp white and black triangular shards, cracked porcelain pieces, paper-like geometric planes, and bold red triangular cutouts that slide across the eyes, cheek, and lips. Large delicate white flowers (cosmos/peony style) bloom and dissolve over the head and face. A small delicate white bird occasionally appears perched on a flower or flying across the composition. Soft smoke and abstract black-and-white fabric shapes swirl around.

Sequence of elegant morphs:
- Start with cracked geometric glasses and floating white cubes
- Transition into flower-crowned face with bird and shattered glass
- Minimalist black/white face with pure white triangles
- Bold red geometric cutouts over the mouth and cheek
- Full floral headdress with bird and red triangle accent
- Abstract fragmented flower-covered face with single red eye
- Cracked flower-over-face composition with flying bird
- Dualistic face with black/white flowers and red diagonal slash
- Final intense geometric shatter with red triangles and floating petals

Ultra-detailed skin texture, dramatic high-contrast lighting, dark abstract background, cinematic depth of field, smooth slow morphing animation, dreamlike and elegant, no text, no watermark.

**Music / audio:**
Dark elegant ethereal ambient track — soft melancholic piano, subtle low strings, atmospheric pads, and delicate glassy textures. Mysterious, sophisticated, slightly haunting mood that perfectly matches the black/white dualism and red accents. Soft dynamic swells that follow the morphing transformations. No vocals, high-quality stereo, cinematic and intimate.

MEET THE AI GIRL WHO PLAYS TENNIS FOR A LIVING — AND SHE'S NEVER LOST

She trains, competes, and racks up wins on camera. The catch: she doesn't exist.

Here's how the "AI athlete" model actually works:

An AI girl persona is built with a consistent face, body, and personality using image/video generation tools. Instead of lifestyle or fashion content, her niche is sport — match highlights, training vlogs, "behind the scenes" prep, rackets and outfits, rivalries with other AI athletes.

The mechanism is simple: physical talent doesn't need to be real, only the narrative around it does. Generated match clips, fake tournament brackets, and AI commentary create a storyline fans follow like a real career.

How she earns:

Sponsorship deals with sportswear/equipment brands looking for cheap, controllable "athletes"
Paid fan subscriptions for exclusive training content and match reactions
Licensing her face/likeness to sports betting or fantasy-sim apps
Selling a personal "AI coach" app trained on her persona
NFT/collectible drops tied to her "career milestones" (Grand Slam wins, rankings)

The twist: her fanbase doesn't care that she's never held a racket — they're not following an athlete, they're following a story that updates on schedule

Something super exciting happened quietly on HF over the past month: AI agents became AI builders, and they did it in the open!

During our ICML reproduction challenge, 1,221 humans teamed up with coding agents to verify and reproduce 2,226 papers. 

But here's the cool part: everything happened on the @huggingface hub: 6,816 reproduction logbooks published openly, 2,962 cloud jobs launched, 35,908 claims judged, all traceable, all public and transparent

For years the hub has been where humans collaborate on models, datasets and demos. Now we watch agents use it the same way: writing logbooks, publishing results, building on each other's work.

Closed labs run evals behind closed doors and ask you to trust the press release. Open science means anyone can check the receipts and now agents can too!

The next million users of the hub might not be human. and that might be the best thing to ever happen to science!

Full write-up about the hackathon: https://t.co/8cgVzzEJnB
